**(CNN)** — Maurice Jarre, the Academy Award-winning composer behind the iconic scores of cinematic classics such as *Doctor Zhivago* and *Lawrence of Arabia*, passed away from cancer on Sunday in Los Angeles. He was 84.

Throughout a distinguished career, Jarre collaborated with several of Hollywood’s most revered directorial luminaries, including John Huston, Alfred Hitchcock, and most notably, David Lean.

Reflecting on his legacy, fellow French composer Alexandre Desplat—who interviewed Jarre at the Berlin International Film Festival last month—told CNN on Monday: "Maurice was an immense artist, an incredible symphonist, a magician of melody, and a benevolent human being."

Jarre earned Academy Awards in 1963 and 1966 for his masterful work on David Lean’s *Lawrence of Arabia* and *Doctor Zhivago*, respectively. Though he garnered six additional Oscar nominations over the course of his career, his third Academy Award came via another fruitful partnership with Lean on the 1984 film *A Passage to India*.

Later in his career, Jarre pivoted from traditional orchestral compositions to become a pioneer of electronic film scoring. He crafted memorable soundtracks for numerous acclaimed films, including *Witness*, *Fatal Attraction*, *Dead Poets Society*, and *Ghost*. Concurrently, his son, Jean-Michel Jarre, rose to international fame as a leading electronic music artist, celebrated for global hits such as "Oxygène" and for his monumental outdoor concerts. Maurice Jarre’s final feature film score was for the 2000 drama *I Dreamed of Africa*.

Although Jarre’s broader body of work encompassed symphonies, ballet, and theater, it was his extraordinary canon of 150 film scores that earned him an honorary Golden Bear at the Berlin International Film Festival last month—nearly half a century after producer Sam Spiegel first hired him for *Lawrence of Arabia*.

In a statement released late last year, festival director Dieter Kosslick remarked: "Film composers often operate in the shadows of acclaimed directors and movie stars. With Maurice Jarre, it is different; the music of *Doctor Zhivago*, like so much of his work, is world-famous and remains unforgettable in the history of cinema."

During his appearance in Berlin, speaking with two-time Oscar nominee Desplat (who scored *The Queen* and *The Curious Case of Benjamin Button*), Jarre reflected on his professional relationships: "I never really had a 'bust-up' with a good director. The world of cinema has lost one of its most luminous and transformative musical voices. Following his death from cancer at the age of 84, renowned composer Maurice Jarre is being remembered not only as a master of Hollywood’s golden age, but as a fearless musical innovator whose work shaped the emotional landscape of film for more than half a century. Over a staggering career that spanned more than 150 feature films, Jarre redefined what a movie score could achieve, seamlessly evolving from the grandeur of traditional orchestral arrangements to the cutting-edge possibilities of electronic music.

Born in Lyon, France, in 1924, Jarre initially studied engineering before following his passion for music at the prestigious Conservatoire de Paris. He honed his craft as a percussionist and director for the Théâtre National Populaire, an experience that instilled in him a deep understanding of dramatic tension and theatrical storytelling. When he transitioned to cinema, this background allowed him to write scores that were not merely background accompaniment, but active narrative forces.

Jarre’s rise to international stardom was cemented through his legendary collaboration with director David Lean. In 1962, Jarre was given just six weeks to compose the music for *Lawrence of Arabia*. The resulting score—a majestic blend of sweeping strings, exotic scales, and thunderous percussion—became an instant classic, capturing the terrifying beauty and vastness of the desert. It earned Jarre his first Academy Award and established him as Hollywood’s premier composer for epics. 

He would go on to win two more Oscars: one for *Doctor Zhivago* (1965), which featured the hauntingly romantic, balalaika-driven "Lara’s Theme" (a melody that became a global pop phenomenon), and another for *A Passage to India* (1984).

Yet, what truly set Jarre apart from many of his contemporaries was his refusal to be boxed in by his own success. While many composers of his stature remained tethered to traditional symphony orchestras, Jarre embraced technological evolution. In the 1980s, he emerged as a pioneer of electronic film music, integrating synthesizers and acoustic instruments in groundbreaking ways. 

His Oscar-nominated score for Peter Weir’s *Witness* (1985)—composed entirely with synthesizers—is widely considered a landmark in electronic scoring, highlighted by the hypnotic, rhythmic build of the famous barn-building sequence. He continued this bold exploration in films like *The Year of Living Dangerously* (1982), *Fatal Attraction* (1987), and *Dead Poets Society* (1989), proving that electronic soundscapes could convey just as much warmth, dread, and humanity as a 90-piece orchestra.

Throughout his prolific life, Jarre collaborated with cinema's greatest directors, including John Huston, Luchino Visconti, Alfred Hitchcock, and George Miller. His immense contributions to the arts were recognized globally; just weeks before his passing, he was awarded the prestigious Lifetime Achievement Golden Bear at the Berlin International Film Festival, a fitting honor for a man who spent decades soundtracking human emotion.

Maurice Jarre leaves behind a rich musical legacy that bridged continents, genres, and generations—a legacy that lives on through his son, electronic music pioneer Jean-Michel Jarre, and in the timeless melodies that continue to move moviegoers around the globe. Jarre died in Los Angeles following a battle with cancer, his manager confirmed Monday.

Jarre’s rise to international renown was inextricably linked with Lean. The duo first teamed up for 1962’s "Lawrence of Arabia," where Jarre’s thunderous percussion and dramatic, sweeping strings captured the vastness of the Arabian desert. The score earned Jarre his first Oscar and remains one of the most recognizable themes in film history. 

They struck gold again three years later with "Doctor Zhivago" (1965). The soundtrack produced "Lara's Theme," an international pop phenomenon that topped the charts and earned Jarre his second Academy Award. Jarre would secure his third Oscar for Lean’s 1984 period drama, "A Passage to India."

"I was always trying to give a film its own voice," Jarre once said of his process. "With David Lean, the music was never just background—it was another character."

### Embracing the Electronic Frontier

While Jarre built his early reputation on grand, symphonic orchestrations, he startled critics and audiences in the 1980s by boldly pivoting toward electronic scoring. Rather than viewing synthesizers as a threat to traditional orchestras, Jarre embraced them as a powerful new palette.

His electronic score for Peter Weir’s 1985 thriller "Witness"—notably the celebrated "barn building" sequence—earned him another Oscar nomination and demonstrated his uncanny ability to blend traditional drama with modern, minimalist acoustic sounds. He continued his exploration of electronic textures in hits like "The Year of Living Dangerously" (1982), "Fatal Attraction" (1987), and "Dead Poets Society" (1989), proving his versatility across genres and eras.

Remarkably, electronic music ran in the family: Jarre was the father of Jean-Michel Jarre, the French electronic music pioneer famed for landmark synthesizer albums like *Oxygène*.

Jarre’s death comes just weeks after he received one of the highest honors of his career. In February, the composer made his final public appearance at the 59th Berlin International Film Festival, where he was awarded an Honorary Golden Bear for Lifetime Achievement.

During the ceremony, festival director Dieter Kosslick paid tribute to Jarre, declaring that "film composers are often in the shadow of great directors... Maurice Jarre was a giant who brought those images to life."

Born in Lyon, France, in 1924, Jarre originally studied engineering before enrolling at the Conservatoire de Paris to study percussion and composition. He spent his early career writing music for French theater before moving to Hollywood in the 1960s.

Jarre is survived by his wife, Fong F. Chow; his sons, Jean-Michel and Kevin; and his daughter, Stéfanie.

March 30, 2009 -- Updated 1842 GMT (0242 HKT)

**(CNN)** -- Maurice Jarre, the legendary French composer who swept moviegoers across vast deserts and icy Russian plains with his iconic, Oscar-winning film scores, has died in Los Angeles. He was 84.

Jarre died in his sleep late Saturday night following a battle with cancer, according to his manager, Bernard Miyet. 

Over a career spanning more than five decades, Jarre composed music for over 150 films, working alongside cinematic titans such as David Lean, John Huston, and Peter Weir. 

He was a three-time Academy Award winner, taking home Oscars for best original score for David Lean's epics "Lawrence of Arabia" (1962), "Doctor Zhivago" (1965), and "A Passage to India" (1984).

[WATCH: A look back at Maurice Jarre's most memorable film scores]

French President Nicolas Sarkozy paid tribute to Jarre on Sunday, calling him a "giant" of film music.

"Maurice Jarre was not only a great composer, he was a visionary who left an indelible mark on the history of world cinema," Sarkozy said in a statement released by his office. "By choosing to work with the greatest directors in the world, he proved that music could elevate cinema into a transcendent art form."

**A master of epic soundscapes**

Born in Lyon, France, in 1924, Jarre initially studied engineering before pursuing music at the Paris Conservatoire against his father's wishes. He began his career as a percussionist and theater director before transitioning to film composition in the 1950s.

His breakthrough came when British director David Lean hired him to score "Lawrence of Arabia." Given just six weeks to write the music, Jarre crafted a sweeping, dramatically percussion-heavy theme that captured both the grand scale and the haunting solitude of the desert. The score remains one of the most famous in cinematic history.

"I had no time, no sleep, but I had the inspiration of Lean's incredible images," Jarre recalled in a 2004 interview with CNN. "When you see pictures like that, the music writes itself."

[Watch tribute: Hollywood directors remember working with Maurice Jarre]

Jarre was also known for his versatility. While celebrated for grand orchestral arrangements—such as "Lara's Theme" from "Doctor Zhivago," which became a global pop hit—he was an early adopter of electronic synths in film scoring during the 1980s. He used electronic music to tense, atmospheric effect in films like Peter Weir's "Witness" (1985) and "The Year of Living Dangerously" (1982), as well as Adrian Lyne's psychological thriller "Fatal Attraction" (1987).

His later hits included the poignant, sweeping score for the 1989 hit "Dead Poets Society," which earned him a BAFTA award.

**A musical dynasty**

Jarre received a lifetime achievement award at the Berlin International Film Festival in February 2009, making his final public appearance to accept the honor.

He is survived by his wife, Fui Fong Khaw, and his three children, including electronic music pioneer Jean-Michel Jarre, set designer Stéfanie Jarre, and screenwriter Kevin Jarre.

Funeral services will be held in Los Angeles in a private ceremony, the family said.

*CNN's Per Nyberg and Richard Allen Greene contributed to this report.*
